Allosauria.description: Allosauria is a clade of allosauroid theropod dinosaurs named by Paul in 1988. Carrano and colleagues revised it in 2012.

dispute.summary: The content and rank of Eutitanosauria, and its position relative to Lithostrotia, vary among analyses. Sanz and colleagues (1999) introduced the name for a clade of advanced titanosaurs, and Carballido and colleagues (2022) redefined it as the node of Patagotitan and Saltasaurus, whose two stems are Colossosauria and Saltasauroidea. Whether that node lies within Lithostrotia depends on the position of Malawisaurus: in most analyses Lithostrotia includes nearly all titanosaurs, but in others it is the sister of Colossosauria and so falls within Eutitanosauria (Carballido and colleagues, 2022). Its content is highly labile among analyses, and many studies neither define nor label it (Carballido and colleagues, 2022). It is placed within Lithostrotia, following the majority topology.

dispute.summary: The monophyly of Parankylosauria is contested. Soto-Acuña and colleagues (2021) erected it for Stegouros, Antarctopelta, and Kunbarrasaurus and recovered it across five matrices, with support from Soto-Acuña and colleagues (2024). Using a different matrix, Maidment and colleagues (2025) did not recover the clade and instead dispersed its putative members across Ankylosauria and Thyreophora. Whether it is a genuine clade sister to Euankylosauria or a convergent Gondwanan grade remains open; Patagopelta and Minmi are contested members placed elsewhere.

Acanthopholis.description: Acanthopholis (meaning "spiny scale") is a genus of nodosaurid ankylosaur dinosaur of uncertain placement within Nodosauridae, now considered a nomen dubium, named by Huxley in 1867. It lived during the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now the United Kingdom, in the West Melbury Marly Chalk. Its only species is Acanthopholis horrida. It was described from scutes and spines of dermal armor, three teeth, fragmentary vertebrae, partial skull, and distal end of a humerus. Acanthopholis was a quadrupedal herbivore estimated at 3 to 5.5 meters long.

Acrocanthosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'akros' meaning 'high', 'akantha' meaning 'spine', and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', referring to its high-spined vertebrae.
diagnostic_features: Massive and greatly elongated neural spines throughout cervical and dorsal vertebrae
Medial caudal vertebrae with supplementary (double) neural processes
Anterior chevrons closed proximally by transverse bar and bearing an upward-projecting anterior process on each ramus
Tibia strongly bowed outward, more so than in any known allied genus
Metatarsal III somewhat constricted proximally by lateral elements (metatarsals II and IV)

synonyms.name: Acracanthus
synonyms.reason: Name appears in a dissertation, which does not meet ICZN publication requirements; referable to Acrocanthosaurus. Per Olshevsky's Dinosaur Genera List.

species.name: Acrocanthosaurus atokensis
species.etymology: Named for Atoka County, Oklahoma, where the type was found.

type_specimen.material: Partial skeleton with skull-roof and braincase elements and partial left mandible, nine cervical plus dorsal and caudal vertebrae, ribs, gastralia, coracoid, pubes, ischium, and fragmentary hindlimb bones

notable_specimens.institution: North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences
notable_specimens.significance: Most complete and largest known skeleton, with the only complete skull and forelimb. Its braincase enabled CT brain and inner-ear reconstruction, and the intact forelimb allowed the first study of arm range of motion and predatory function.

notable_specimens.institution: National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution
notable_specimens.significance: Subadult identified in 2024 as the first definitive record of the genus from eastern North America. The most completely known theropod from the Arundel Formation, previously misidentified as an ornithomimosaur, and the smallest known individual of the genus.

notable_specimens.institution: Shuler Museum of Paleontology, Southern Methodist University
notable_specimens.significance: A partial skeleton missing most of the skull from the Twin Mountains Formation of Texas, one of the first much more complete specimens described in the 1990s; now part of the Fort Worth Museum of Science and History collection.

notable_specimens.institution: Museum of Paleontology, University of Michigan
notable_specimens.significance: A juvenile partial skeleton that established the presence of the genus in the Cloverly Formation of Wyoming in 2012. Found near the shoulder blade of a Sauroposeidon in a Bighorn Basin bonebed.

Acrocanthosaurus.description: Acrocanthosaurus is a genus of carcharodontosaurid theropod dinosaur named by Stovall and Langston in 1950. It lived during the Aptian to Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous in what is now the United States, in the Antlers Formation. Its only species is Acrocanthosaurus atokensis. Acrocanthosaurus was a bipedal carnivore estimated at 11 to 12.2 meters long. A well-known specimen is nicknamed "Fran".

Adeopapposaurus.etymology: From Greek 'adeo' meaning 'to eat one's fill' (or 'far'), 'pappo' meaning 'grandfather' or possibly 'eating', and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'far eating lizard', referring to its long neck
diagnostic_features: Series of large foramina in a sub-vertical row on the lateral surface of the premaxilla.
Strongly rugose depression bordered by a protuberance with a series of foramina in a sub-vertical row on the lateral surface of the anterior end of the dentary.
Eleven anteroposteriorly elongated cervical vertebrae.
Thirteen dorsal vertebrae with neural arches taller than their respective centra.

species.name: Adeopapposaurus mognai
species.etymology: Named for the Mogna locality in San Juan, Argentina, where the fossils were found.

location.notes: Martínez (2009) places the holotype in the "Upper Pelitic Member", 148 m from the base, in an earlier scheme; Martínez and Colombi (2011) divide the formation into lower, middle and upper members and name the middle member's pelitic facies as the source of Adeopapposaurus.

type_specimen.institution: División de Paleontología de Vertebrados del Museo de Ciencias Naturales y Universidad Nacional de San Juan
type_specimen.material: Incomplete skeleton: complete skull with mandible in occlusion; complete cervical, dorsal, and sacral vertebral series; nine articulated caudal vertebrae with chevrons; pectoral girdle; forelimbs; incomplete pelvic girdle and hindlimbs.

Adeopapposaurus.description: Adeopapposaurus (meaning "far eating lizard") is a genus of massospondylid sauropodomorph dinosaur named by Martínez in 2009. It lived during the Hettangian to Toarcian stages of the Early Jurassic in what is now Argentina, in the Cañón del Colorado Formation. Its only species is Adeopapposaurus mognai. Adeopapposaurus was a bipedal herbivore estimated at about 2.9 meters long.

Agilisaurus.etymology: From Latin 'agilis' meaning 'agile' and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', meaning 'agile lizard'.
diagnostic_features: Middle part of parietal strongly contracted
Nasal long with longitudinal depression at central suture
Posterior process of premaxilla does not contact the lacrimal
Palpebral bone well-developed, posterior end abutting lateral surface of postorbital, dividing orbit into upper and lower openings
Elliptical foramen present on lateral surface of femoral shaft distal to fourth trochanter
Obturator process of ischium positioned at proximal third of shaft

species.name: Agilisaurus louderbacki
species.etymology: Named for the late U.S. geologist Dr. George D. Louderback, who in 1915 was the first scientist to discover dinosaur fossils in the Sichuan Basin.

type_specimen.material: Nearly complete skeleton lacking only portions of the left forelimb and left hindlimb

references.authors: Peng, G.
references.title: Jurassic ornithopod Agilisaurus louderbacki (Ornithopoda: Fabrosauridae) from Zigong, Sichuan, China

Agilisaurus.description: Agilisaurus (meaning "agile lizard") is a genus of neornithischian dinosaur named by Peng in 1992. It lived during the Bajocian to Oxfordian stages of the Middle Jurassic and the Late Jurassic in what is now China, in the Shaximiao Formation. Its only species is Agilisaurus louderbacki. It was described from a nearly complete skeleton lacking only portions of the left forelimb and left hindlimb. Agilisaurus was a bipedal herbivore estimated at 1.2 to 1.7 meters long.

Allosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'allos' meaning 'different' or 'other' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'different lizard', alluding to its lightweight vertebrae
diagnostic_features: Vertebral centra deeply excavated on the sides to reduce weight, producing an hourglass form in some elements
Vertebrae biconcave with shallow cavities, centra not pneumatic but greatly lightened by lateral excavations
Anterior caudal centrum so strongly constricted that its least transverse diameter (38 mm) is far less than its anterior face diameter (90 mm)
Foot bones very slender

synonyms.name: Antrodemus
synonyms.reason: Although described before Allosaurus, the type material is too poor to be diagnostic; Allosaurus is given priority and Antrodemus treated as a junior synonym.

synonyms.name: Wyomingraptor
synonyms.reason: Coined by an anonymous caller on Dr. Bob's Dinofacts radio show; never officially described in scientific literature.

synonyms.name: Labrosaurus
synonyms.reason: Type material is now considered indistinguishable from Allosaurus.

synonyms.name: Creosaurus
synonyms.reason: Williston (1901) noted that Marsh had never adequately distinguished Creosaurus from Allosaurus; subsequent work has confirmed the synonymy.

synonyms.name: Madsenius
synonyms.reason: Informal name; never met ICZN requirements for formal publication and is treated as referable to Allosaurus. Per Olshevsky's Dinosaur Genera List.

iczn_cases.notes: Designated USNM 4734 as the neotype of Allosaurus fragilis, conserving usage (Opinion 2486, Case 3506); replaces the non-diagnostic original syntype YPM 1930.

species.name: Allosaurus fragilis
species.etymology: From Latin 'fragilis' meaning 'fragile', referring to the lightweight construction features of the vertebrae that Othniel Charles Marsh noted when describing the species in 1877.

type_specimen.institution: National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution
type_specimen.material: Nearly complete skeleton including the skull and lower jaws, presacral vertebrae, a complete sacrum, about thirty caudal vertebrae, the pelvis, ribs, and all four limbs and feet.

synonyms.name: Epanterias amplexus
synonyms.reason: Based on AMNH 5767; generally treated as a junior synonym of Allosaurus fragilis, though debate persists. Epanterias is also widely considered nomen dubium due to lack of diagnostic features.

species.name: Allosaurus jimmadseni
species.etymology: Honors James H. Madsen Jr., for work excavating, preparing, and curating Cleveland-Lloyd Allosaurus material.

type_specimen.material: Nearly complete articulated skeleton: left half of skull with occluded mandible, cervical-caudal vertebral column, ribs, gastral basket, pectoral girdle and forelimb, complete pelvis, hindlimbs, and partial pes.

diagnostic_features: Ventral margin of the jugal is virtually straight, lacking the pronounced sigmoidal convexity present in A. fragilis
Nasals bear paired, blade-like crests along their lateral margins forming a pronounced nasolacrimal crest, absent in A. fragilis
A row of neurovascular foramina pierces the medioventral wall of the maxillary antorbital fossa
Relatively taller lacrimal horns than in A. fragilis
Straight posteroventral jugal ramus of the maxilla where it articulates with the jugal, rather than the pronounced ventral deflection seen in A. fragilis
Axial intercentrum is rotated dorsally and has a flared rim in lateral view
species.authors: Chure, D. J.; Loewen, M. A.

notable_specimens.significance: A 95 percent complete, partially articulated subadult, one of the most famous Allosaurus specimens. Renowned for its 19 broken or infected bones, including a long-lived foot infection that may have contributed to its death; later referred to A. jimmadseni.

A second well-preserved Allosaurus from Howe Ranch. Preserves a 20 by 20 centimeter skin impression at the base of the tail showing large scales up to 2 centimeters across, though the scales resemble sauropod skin and associated non-theropod remains cast some doubt on the attribution.

Found in 1879 but left unpacked until 1903, when it proved to be one of the most complete theropod specimens then known. Put on view in 1908 as the first free-standing mount of a theropod dinosaur, famously posed as if scavenging an Apatosaurus, though never scientifically described.
The largest definitive Allosaurus specimen, estimated at about 9.7 meters long and 2.3 to 2.7 tonnes, used to anchor maximum-size estimates for the genus.

Allosaurus.description: Allosaurus (meaning "different lizard") is a genus of allosaurid theropod dinosaur named by Marsh in 1877. It lived during the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic in what is now the United States, in the Morrison Formation. It contains 2 species, of which Allosaurus fragilis is the type species. Gilmore redescribed it in 1920. In 2023 the ICZN designated a new type specimen for it (Opinion 2486). Allosaurus was a bipedal carnivore estimated at about 8.5 meters long. Well-known specimens include "Big Al" and "Big Al II".

Anhuilong.etymology: Named after Anhui province in China combined with Chinese 'long' meaning 'dragon'; meaning 'Anhui dragon'
diagnostic_features: Lateral edge of deltopectoral crest turns caudolaterally (differs from other mamenchisaurids).
Lateral accessory process of humerus more robust than medial one (reversed from other Mamenchisauridae).
Ratio of total length of radius to humerus is 0.50, the lowest value among mamenchisaurids.
Ratio of total length of ulna to humerus is 0.56, the lowest value among mamenchisaurids.
Elliptical cross-sectional shape of ulna at mid-shaft with highest transverse-to-craniocaudal diameter ratio among mamenchisaurids.
Nearly perpendicular orientation of proximal end of ulna relative to long axis of ulnar shaft.

species.name: Anhuilong diboensis
species.etymology: Named for the locality where the holotype is reposited.

type_specimen.institution: Geological and Paleontological Museum of Anhui
type_specimen.material: Associated and complete left humerus, ulna and radius of an individual.

references.title: The second mamenchisaurid dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic of Eastern China

Anhuilong.description: Anhuilong (meaning "Anhui dragon") is a genus of mamenchisaurid sauropod dinosaur named by Ren and colleagues in 2020. It lived during the Middle Jurassic in what is now China, in the Hongqin Formation. Its only species is Anhuilong diboensis. It was described from associated and complete left humerus, ulna and radius of an individual. Anhuilong was a quadrupedal herbivore.

Antarctopelta.etymology: From 'Antarctica' and Greek 'pelta' meaning 'shield', meaning 'Antarctic shield', reflecting its discovery in Antarctica.
diagnostic_features: Asymmetrical cheek teeth with at least seven denticles on the mesial border, marked vertical ridges confluent with the denticles on the lingual side, and an ornamented cingulum with fine striations.
Scapular girdle unfused (scapula and coracoid not coossified).
Metatarsal IV with a proximal epiphysis noticeably wider than those of the other metatarsals.
Well-marked striations on the supracetabular shelf of the ilium.
Sacral shield filling the space between both ilia and covering the sacral neural spines, ornamented with several irregular sulci and pits.
Intradermal ossicles approximately 8 mm in diameter.

species.name: Antarctopelta oliveroi
species.etymology: Named for Eduardo Olivero, the Argentine geologist who discovered the holotype in 1986 and has worked in Antarctica for decades.

type_specimen.material: Partial skeleton: left dentary fragment with an erupting tooth and at least five isolated cheek teeth; anterior, mid (cast), and posterior cervical vertebrae; two fused dorsosacral and three sacral centra; ~eight caudal vertebrae; rib fragments; left scapular girdle; distal radius; ilium fragments; metatarsal epiphyses; two pedal phalanges; dorsal and costal osteoderms; sacral-shield fragments; caudal-weapon osteoderms; and ossicles.

references.title: A new look at the first dinosaur discovered in Antarctica: reappraisal of Antarctopelta oliveroi (Ankylosauria: Parankylosauria)
references.notes: Full redescription of the holotype; recovers Antarctopelta within Parankylosauria, confirms an upper Campanian age, and reinterprets the caudal osteoderms as a Stegouros-like tail weapon.

Antarctopelta.description: Antarctopelta (meaning "Antarctic shield") is a genus of parankylosaurian ankylosaur dinosaur named by Salgado and Gasparini in 2006. It lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Antarctica, in the Snow Hill Island Formation. Its only species is Antarctopelta oliveroi. Soto-Acuña and colleagues redescribed it in 2024. Antarctopelta was a quadrupedal herbivore estimated at about 4 meters long.

Apatodon.etymology: From Greek 'apate' ('deceit') and 'odon' ('tooth'), for the original misidentification of the specimen as the jaw of a mammal.

species.name: Apatodon mirus
species.etymology: From Latin 'mirus' ('wonderful', 'astonishing'), for the unexpected character of the specimen as Marsh interpreted it.

location.notes: Where the type came from was never recorded. Marsh (1877) gives only the Rocky Mountain region and a horizon of Lower Cretaceous or Jurassic, and Chure (2000) reports the holotype lost and repeats the same phrase. The Morrison Formation and a Colorado attribution appear in later compilations without stated support.

type_specimen.material: Weathered fragment of a dinosaurian vertebra, from the neural spine, originally described as a portion of a lower jaw with the last molar in place.

references.authors: Marsh, O. C.
references.title: Notice of some new vertebrate fossils
references.notes: Erects the genus and species on a fragment from the Rocky Mountain region, interpreting it as a mammalian lower jaw and giving the horizon as Lower Cretaceous or Jurassic.

references.authors: Chure, D. J.
references.title: A new species of Allosaurus from the Morrison Formation of Dinosaur National Monument (UT-CO) and a revision of the theropod family Allosauridae

references.title: A revision of the parainfraclass Archosauria Cope, 1869, excluding the advanced Crocodylia

Apatodon.description: Apatodon is a genus of dinosaurian dinosaur of uncertain placement within Dinosauria, now considered a nomen dubium, named by Marsh in 1877. It lived during the Early Jurassic, the Middle Jurassic, the Late Jurassic and the Early Cretaceous in what is now the United States. Its only species is Apatodon mirus.

dispute.summary: Australotitan is recovered within Diamantinasauria, where Beeston and colleagues (2024) found insufficient autapomorphies to distinguish it from Diamantinasaurus and suggested it is probably a junior synonym of Diamantinasaurus matildae, retaining it conservatively as an indeterminate diamantinasaurian.

Australotitan.etymology: From Latin 'australis' meaning 'southern' and Greek 'titan' meaning 'giant', referring to the large size of this dinosaur from southern Australia.
diagnostic_features: Ulna with heavily reduced anterolateral and olecranon processes relative to much enlarged and elongate anteromedial process.

Ulna with a distinct radial interosseous ridge within the distal half of the radial fossa, and anterolateral process bearing a distal accessory projection proximal to a proximally beveled distal epiphysis.
Humerus with a rounded ridge extending from the distal end of the deltopectoral crest to just proximal of a tri-lobate distal epiphysis.
Distal ischial blades curve ventrally to produce a dorsal face that is posteriorly directed.
Femur with a medially sloped proximolateral margin, anteroposteriorly narrow diaphysis, and distal condyles directed anterolaterally to posteromedially.

species.name: Australotitan cooperensis
species.etymology: Named for the Cooper-Eromanga Basin, the Cooper Creek system and "Cooper Country", where it was found.

type_specimen.material: Ten appendicular elements: partial left scapula, partial left and complete right humerus, right ulna, right and left pubes and ischia, partial right and left femora, plus corticocancellous internal bone fragments.

species.authors: Hocknull, S. A.; Wilkinson, M.; Lawrence, R. A.; Konstantinov, V.; Mackenzie, S.; Mackenzie, R.

notable_specimens.significance: Referred specimen representing the largest known individual; its 2.146 meter femur is the basis cited for Australotitan being the largest known Australian dinosaur, comparable to Futalognkosaurus and Dreadnoughtus. Preserves femur, ulna, vertebrae, and ribs.

references.title: Meet Australia's largest dinosaur -- Australotitan, the southern titan!

Australotitan.description: Australotitan is a genus of diamantinasaurian sauropod dinosaur named by Hocknull and colleagues in 2021. It lived during the Cenomanian to Turonian stages of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Australia, in the Winton Formation. Its only species is Australotitan cooperensis. Australotitan was a quadrupedal herbivore estimated at about 24 meters long. A well-known specimen is nicknamed "George". Aspects of its classification are disputed.

Daspletosaurus.etymology: From Greek daspletos ('frightful') + sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'frightful lizard'.
diagnostic_features: Premaxilla does not contact nasal below external naris.
Lacrimal 'horn' triangular in lateral aspect, with apex centered above antorbital ramus of bone; exceeds postorbital 'horn' in development.
Neural spine of fourth cervical vertebra much larger than that of fifth; spine of fifth distally pointed.
In adults humerus length estimated equal to 38 per cent of femur length; forelimb powerfully developed.
Anterodistal condyle of metacarpal I reduced, causing first digit to diverge distally from second.
In adults circumference of femur equals 38 to 41 per cent of femur length.

species.name: Daspletosaurus torosus
species.etymology: From Latin 'torosus' meaning 'muscular' or 'brawny', a reference to the animal's robust build.

location.notes: Russell (1970) gives the type as from "quarry 88 of Sternberg 1905", under a pre-1993 Oldman Formation. Powers and colleagues (2026) list CMN 8506 at their quarry Q072, which they call the type locality, 3.867 m below the nearest Oldman-Dinosaur Park Formation contact.

type_specimen.material: Skull and skeleton lacking hind limbs.

species.name: Daspletosaurus horneri
species.etymology: Latinized form of 'Horner', honoring John R. (Jack) Horner for a Two Medicine Formation field program and mentorship.

type_specimen.material: Complete skull, partial pectoral limb, and nearly complete hindlimb.

diagnostic_features: Skull taller than in D. torosus, with a shorter rostral ramus of the lacrimal relative to the ventral ramus (rostral ramus longer in D. torosus).
Antorbital fossa of the lacrimal confluent with the ventral ramus of the bone (separated by a deep concavity in D. torosus).
Coronoid region of the surangular facing more laterally than dorsally (facing equally dorsally and laterally in D. torosus).
Primary lacrimal cornual process lower and less prominent, about 53% the height of the rostral ramus (about 69% in D. torosus).
Pneumatic foramen penetrating the lateral surface of the quadratojugal.

Daspletosaurus.description: Daspletosaurus (meaning "frightful lizard") is a genus of tyrannosaurine theropod dinosaur named by Russell in 1970. It lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Canada and the United States, in the Oldman, Two Medicine and Judith River formations. It contains 3 species, of which Daspletosaurus torosus is the type species. It was described from a skull and skeleton lacking hind limbs. Daspletosaurus was a bipedal carnivore estimated at 8.5 to 11 meters long. Well-known specimens include "Pete III" and "Gorgeous George".

Nanotyrannus.etymology: Originally proposed by Bakker, Williams and Currie (1988) as Latin nano ("small") plus tyrannus ("tyrant"); the derivation is now usually corrected to Greek nanos ("dwarf" or "pygmy") and tyrannos ("king"), in reference to the small body size relative to other tyrannosauroids.

dispute.summary: The validity of Nanotyrannus is actively contested. After the 1988 erection of the genus, Carr (1999) and Woodward and colleagues (2020) argued that the holotype CMNH 7541 is an immature Tyrannosaurus rex, citing tooth-grain immaturity and femoral osteohistology. Longrich and Saitta (2024), Zanno and Napoli (2025) — who erected a second species, N. lethaeus — and Griffin and colleagues (2025, ceratobranchial histology) reaffirmed Nanotyrannus as a distinct, skeletally mature taxon. No broad consensus yet.

diagnostic_features: Muzzle width greatly constricted, only one fourth the width of the temporal region.
Extraordinarily wide basicranium between basitubera and basipterygoid processes.
Two large pneumatic foramina placed one behind the other near the midline of the basisphenoid.
Dorsal surface of the nasal lacks strong ridges and striae.
Parietal wing of the occiput with a sharp angle between dorsal and lateral edges.
Basicranial boxwork with flat ventral floor.

Tarbosaurus.etymology: From Ancient Greek 'tarbos' meaning 'terror' or 'alarm' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.

dispute.summary: The generic placement of the single Mongolian species is long debated. Maleev (1955) named the type material Tyrannosaurus bataar (holotype PIN 551-1) and, in a companion paper, erected Tarbosaurus for the related Tarbosaurus efremovi. Rozhdestvensky (1965) interpreted Maleev's several Mongolian species as growth stages of one animal and, keeping the genus Tarbosaurus, coined the combination Tarbosaurus bataar. Carpenter (1992) judged the differences from Tyrannosaurus to fall within normal individual and ontogenetic variation and sank Tarbosaurus into Tyrannosaurus (Tyrannosaurus bataar), whereas Olshevsky, Ford and Yamamoto (1995) instead split the material among Tarbosaurus, Jenghizkhan and Maleevosaurus. Most work since 1999 recognizes a single species; the majority retains Tarbosaurus bataar, with a minority (e.g. Carr and others) treating it as Tyrannosaurus bataar.

diagnostic_features: Large skull, massive, with 2 large premaxillary foramina and third small foramen between premaxilla and maxilla
Pisolitic orbits
Maxilla long, raised, equipped with powerful saber-like teeth, slightly compressed and serrated marginally
Short neck consisting of 8-9 opisthocoelous cervical vertebrae
Forelimbs extremely reduced; humerus very short with strong deltopectoral crest; proportion of humerus to scapula 3:1
Pubic symphysis strongly elongate anteriorly and curved ventrally forming powerful bony foot

Tarbosaurus.description: Tarbosaurus is a genus of tyrannosaurine theropod dinosaur named by Maleev in 1955. It lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Mongolia, in the Nemegt Formation. Its only species is Tarbosaurus bataar, first named Tyrannosaurus bataar. Tyrannosaurus.etymology: From Greek tyrannos (tyrant) and sauros (lizard); meaning "tyrant lizard", a name Osborn coined to convey the genus's exceptional size relative to all then-known carnivorous land vertebrates.
diagnostic_features: Megalocephalic skull with deep, massively built proportions, brought close to the sacrum by a shortened presacral column of approximately 23 vertebrae.
Fused nasals forming an arched midline ridge on the snout that reinforces the skull against bite-induced stress.
Teeth heterodont and broadly oval to D-shaped in cross-section, with transverse diameter exceeding anteroposterior; alveolar reinforcing plates on the inner surface of the maxilla and dentary.
Squamosal bearing a distinctive horizontal anterior bar projecting into the laterotemporal fenestra.
Forelimb extremely reduced; functionally didactyl manus with powerful recurved unguals; humerus little more than half the length of the femur.
Five sacral vertebrae coossified into a single neural plate with three small fenestrations between S2 and S5.
Pubis, ilium and ischium firmly coalesced; pubis terminating distally in a hugely expanded pedicle ("pubic boot").
Caudal series of approximately 53 vertebrae forming a long, flexible balancing tail without the rod-like rigidity of ornithomimids.

Also shows pathologies: a hole penetrating its jugal and severe tail trauma with bone remodeling.

references.authors: Olshevsky, G.; Ford, T. L.; Yamamoto, S.
references.title: The origin and evolution of the tyrannosaurids (Part 1)

Tyrannosaurus.description: Tyrannosaurus (meaning "tyrant lizard") is a genus of tyrannosaurine theropod dinosaur named by Osborn in 1905. It lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now the United States, in the Hell Creek Formation. Its only species is Tyrannosaurus rex. It was described from a partial skeleton with both jaws and portions of the skull, vertebrae, ribs, scapula, humerus, ilium, pubis, ischium, and metapodials. Tyrannosaurus bataar, first named in Tyrannosaurus, is now Tarbosaurus bataar. Tyrannosaurus was a bipedal carnivore estimated at 11.9 to 13 meters long. Well-known specimens include "Sue", "Stan" and "Scotty".

Conques.lithology: variegated mudstone, with lenticular sandstone and limestone
Conques.description: The Conques Formation is a formation of the Tremp Group in Lleida, Spain, dated to the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous. It consists mainly of variegated mudstone, with lenticular sandstone and limestone. Dinosaurs known from it include Abditosaurus, Adynomosaurus and Pareisactus.

references.authors: Prieto-Márquez, A.; Fondevilla, V.; Sellés, A. G.; Wagner, J. R.; Galobart, À.
references.title: Adynomosaurus arcanus, a new lambeosaurine dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Ibero-Armorican Island of the European archipelago
references.notes: Places it in the "Conques Formation and uppermost Maastrichtian" interval. It is one of three formations of the Tremp Group defined and datable only in the eastern Tremp Syncline; facies alone will not separate it from the Talarn, both being red fluvial beds, so the magnetochron does the work — C31r with red fluvial floodplain is this unit, C29r is the Talarn.

references.authors: Augustin, F. J.; Ősi, A.; Csiki-Sava, Z.
references.title: The Rhabdodontidae (Dinosauria, Ornithischia), an enigmatic dinosaur group endemic to the Late Cretaceous European Archipelago
references.notes: Treats it as a member, placing the Pareisactus scapula in "the Upper Cretaceous (lower Maastrichtian) Conques Member of the Tremp Formation in north-eastern Spain".

references.authors: Cuevas, J. L.
references.title: Estratigrafía del "Garumniense" de la Conca de Tremp, Prepirineo de Lérida [Stratigraphy of the "Garumnian" of the Conca de Tremp, Lleida Pre-Pyrenees]
references.notes: Erects the unit as the "Formación Lutitas, Areniscas y Conglomerados de Conques", with the Tossal d'Obà and Basturs Limestones members, in the Tremp Group. The type section is in the Barranco de Basturs, about 400 m thick, of variegated mudstones with lenticular sandstones; the base passes gradually into the Posa Formation and the top passes rapidly into the red mudstones of the Talarn. Gives no age of its own. Source of the lithology.

references.authors: Díez-Canseco, D.; Arz, J. A.; Benito, M. I.; Díaz-Molina, M.; Arenillas, I.
references.title: Tidal influence in redbeds: a palaeoenvironmental and biochronostratigraphic reconstruction of the Lower Tremp Formation (South-Central Pyrenees, Spain) around the Cretaceous/Paleogene boundary
references.notes: Equates the Conques and Talarn formations together with its Lower Red Unit, after Cuevas (1992) and others, and dates that unit from planktonic foraminifera: "In situ assemblages indicate an early to late Maastrichtian age for the Grey Unit and the Lower Red Unit".

references.authors: Fondevilla, V.; Riera, V.; Vila, B.; Sellés, A. G.; Dinarès-Turell, J.; Vicens, E.; Gaete, R.; Oms, O.; Galobart, À.
references.title: Chronostratigraphic synthesis of the latest Cretaceous dinosaur turnover in south-western Europe
references.notes: In the Orcau section of the northern Isona sector, places "the complete La Posa and Conques formations" in the early Maastrichtian, within chron C31r, on foraminiferal zones and magnetostratigraphy, and rejects the late Maastrichtian that earlier work gave them. In the southern Isona sector only the lower part of the formation is dated, likely within C31r.

references.authors: Pujalte, V.; Schmitz, B.
references.title: Revisión de la estratigrafía del Grupo Tremp ("Garumniense", Cuenca de Tremp-Graus, Pirineos meridionales) [Revision of the stratigraphy of the Tremp Group ("Garumnian", Tremp-Graus Basin, southern Pyrenees)]
references.notes: Assigns to the Conques the variegated mudstones at the base of the Esplugafreda section that Cuevas (1992) included in the Talarn, because they lack carbonate paleosols and Microcodium, and labels the formation Maastrichtian.

West Melbury Marly Chalk.lithology: soft marly chalk and hard gray limestone in couplets
West Melbury Marly Chalk.description: The West Melbury Marly Chalk is a formation in Cambridgeshire and Kent, United Kingdom, dated to the Albian to Cenomanian stages of the Early Cretaceous and the Late Cretaceous. It consists mainly of soft marly chalk and hard gray limestone in couplets. It includes the Cambridge Greensand. Dinosaurs known from it include Acanthopholis, Eucercosaurus, Macrurosaurus and Syngonosaurus.

references.authors: Hopson, P. M.
references.title: A stratigraphical framework for the Upper Cretaceous Chalk of England and Scotland, with statements on the Chalk of Northern Ireland and the UK Offshore Sector
references.notes: Defines the formation and names Copt Point among its primary reference sections. Source of the lithology.

references.authors: Barrett, P. M.; Bonsor, J. A.
references.title: A revision of the non-avian dinosaurs 'Eucercosaurus tanyspondylus' and 'Syngonosaurus macrocercus' from the Cambridge Greensand, UK
references.notes: Gives "West Melbury Marly Chalk Formation (Upper Cretaceous; Cenomanian)" and notes that its vertebrate remains are "reworked from the underlying Gault Formation (Lower Cretaceous; upper Albian ...)".

references.authors: Raven, T. J.; Barrett, P. M.; Pond, S. B.; Maidment, S. C. R.
references.title: Osteology and taxonomy of British Wealden Supergroup (Berriasian-Aptian) ankylosaurs (Ornithischia, Ankylosauria)
references.notes: Independently gives "West Melbury Marly Chalk Formation (Cenomanian)".

Antlers.description: The Antlers Formation is a formation of the Trinity Group in Oklahoma, United States, dated to the Aptian to Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous. Dinosaurs known from it include Acrocanthosaurus and Sauroposeidon.

references.authors: D'Emic, M. D.; Melstrom, K. M.; Eddy, D. R.
references.title: Paleobiology and geographic range of the large-bodied Cretaceous theropod dinosaur Acrocanthosaurus atokensis
references.notes: Gives "Antlers Formation (Lower Cretaceous, Aptian-Albian)". D'Emic (2012) records that it is laterally equivalent to the Twin Mountains Formation.

references.authors: Suarez, C. A.; Frederickson, J.; Cifelli, R. L.; Pittman, J. G.; Nydam, R. L.; Hunt-Foster, R. K.; Morgan, K.
references.title: A new vertebrate fauna from the Lower Cretaceous Holly Creek Formation of the Trinity Group, southwest Arkansas, USA
references.notes: Places it within its group by state: in Oklahoma and adjacent Texas the Trinity Group "consists almost entirely of the Antlers Formation, although the Holly Creek Formation is present in extreme southeast McCurtain County".

references.authors: D'Emic, M. D.
references.title: Revision of the sauropod dinosaurs of the Lower Cretaceous Trinity Group, southern USA, with the description of a new genus
references.notes: Gives the Sauroposeidon holotype horizon as "Early Cretaceous (Aptian–Albian) Antlers Formation of southern Oklahoma, USA", and describes the unit as "a lateral equivalent of the Trinity Group of Texas".

Cañón del Colorado.lithology: mudstone, sandy mudstone, conglomerate and sandstone
Cañón del Colorado.description: The Cañón del Colorado Formation is a formation in San Juan, Argentina, dated to the Hettangian to Toarcian stages of the Early Jurassic. It consists mainly of mudstone, sandy mudstone, conglomerate and sandstone. The dinosaur Adeopapposaurus is known from it.

references.authors: Martínez, R. N.
references.title: Adeopapposaurus mognai, gen. et sp. nov. (Dinosauria: Sauropodomorpha), with comments on adaptations of basal Sauropodomorpha
references.notes: Gives the Adeopapposaurus horizon as "the Upper Pelitic Member ... of the Lower Jurassic Cañón del Colorado Formation", from outcrops in the southwestern Sierra de Mogna, San Juan, northwestern Argentina. Gives only the series.

references.notes: Independently gives "the Cañón del Colorado Formation (Lower Jurassic) of Argentina".

references.authors: Apaldetti, C.; Martínez, R. N.; Alcober, O. A.; Pol, D.
references.title: A New Basal Sauropodomorph (Dinosauria: Saurischia) from Quebrada del Barro Formation (Marayes-El Carrizal Basin), Northwestern Argentina
references.notes: Sets it beside the Norian units of the region, the Los Colorados, Laguna Colorada and Quebrada del Barro, as the Lower Jurassic one.

references.authors: Martínez, R. N.; Colombi, C. E.
references.title: Evolución litofacial y edad de la Formación Cañón del Colorado (Jurásico Inferior), Precordillera Oriental, San Juan [Lithofacial evolution and age of the Cañón del Colorado Formation (Lower Jurassic), Eastern Precordillera, San Juan]

references.authors: Milana, J. P.; Martínez, R. N.; Alcober, O. A.
references.title: A new dinosaur locality of Upper Triassic - Lower Jurassic age, from San Juan province, Argentina
references.notes: Reports two specimens of "a new prosauropod of the plateosaurid type" from the formation in the Sierra de Mogna, and leans to a Late Triassic age on regional geology.

Shaximiao.lithology: purplish-red mudstone, sandy mudstone and siltstone, with yellow-gray sandstone interbeds
Shaximiao.description: The Shaximiao Formation is a formation in Sichuan and Chongqing, China, dated to the Bajocian to Tithonian stages of the Middle Jurassic and the Late Jurassic. It consists mainly of purplish-red mudstone, sandy mudstone and siltstone, with yellow-gray sandstone interbeds. It is also known as the Dashanpu. Dinosaurs known from it include Mamenchisaurus, Chialingosaurus, Chungkingosaurus, Huayangosaurus and 24 other genera.

dispute.summary: The age is in flux and the lower and upper parts are dated separately. Mannion and colleagues (2019) record that "Wang et al. (2018) recently dated the Shaximiao (=Dashanpu) Formation as Oxfordian, rather than the late Middle Jurassic (Bathonian-Callovian) age that has been the consensus for some time", and say outright that "the ages of several Jurassic stratigraphic units from China are in a state of flux". Sánchez-Fenollosa and colleagues (2025) split it, giving the lower Shaximiao as "Bathonian-early Oxfordian" and the upper as "?Kimmeridgian-?Tithonian". Xiashaximiao and Shangshaximiao are the lower and upper parts rather than spellings: xia and shang are Chinese for lower and upper.

references.authors: Mannion, P. D.; Upchurch, P.; Schwarz, D.; Wings, O.
references.title: Taxonomic affinities of the putative titanosaurs from the Late Jurassic Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania: phylogenetic and biogeographic implications for eusauropod dinosaur evolution
references.journal: Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society
references.notes: Records Wang and colleagues' (2018) Oxfordian redating and the consensus it displaces, "the late Middle Jurassic (Bathonian-Callovian) age that has been the consensus for some time", and gives Dashanpu as an equivalent name.

references.authors: Sánchez-Fenollosa, S.; Cobos, A.
references.title: New insights into the phylogeny and skull evolution of stegosaurian dinosaurs: an extraordinary cranium from the European Late Jurassic (Dinosauria: Stegosauria)
references.notes: Dates the two parts separately, lower "Bathonian-early Oxfordian" and upper "?Kimmeridgian-?Tithonian", both hedged in the source.

references.authors: Sadleir, R.; Barrett, P. M.; Powell, H. P.
references.title: The anatomy and systematics of Eustreptospondylus oxoniensis, a theropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic of Oxfordshire, England
references.notes: Uses "Lower Shaximiao Formation (Bajocian or Bathonian-Callovian)", the oldest bound among the sources cited.

references.authors: Li, K.; Liu, J.; Yang, C.; Hu, F.
references.title: Dinosaur assemblages from the Middle Jurassic Shaximiao Formation and Chuanjie Formation in the Sichuan-Yunnan Basin, China
references.notes: Argues that "the entire Shaximiao Formation is of Bajocian-Callovian age (middle-late part of Middle Jurassic)", putting the upper member "of Middle Jurassic age (Bathonian-Callovian)" in the abstract but "namely the Bajocian-Bathonian" in the discussion. It records the reading it argues against: the invertebrates placed the formation in the Middle Jurassic, "although vertebrate fossils tended to indicate a Late Jurassic age for the upper member of the Shaximiao Formation". Source of the lithology.

references.authors: Buffetaut, E.; Suteethorn, V.
references.title: The dinosaur fauna of the Sao Khua Formation of Thailand and the beginning of the Cretaceous radiation of dinosaurs in Asia
references.notes: Treats the lower and upper parts as separate formations of different ages, contrasting the Sao Khua sauropods with "the increasingly well known sauropods from the Middle Jurassic Xiashaximiao Formation and the Late Jurassic Shanshaximiao Formation of China".

references.authors: Wang, J.; Ye, Y.; Pei, R.; Tian, Y.; Feng, C.; Zheng, D.; Chang, S. C.
references.title: Age of Jurassic basal sauropods in Sichuan, China: A reappraisal of basal sauropod evolution
references.notes: Cited by Mannion and colleagues (2019) for redating the Shaximiao Formation as Oxfordian.

Morrison.description: The Morrison Formation is a formation in the United States, dated to the Oxfordian to Berriasian stages of the Late Jurassic and the Early Cretaceous. It is also known as the Atlantosaurus beds. It includes the Brushy Basin Member, the Kenton Member, the Salt Wash Member and the Tidwell Member. Dinosaurs known from it include Allosaurus, Camarasaurus, Diplodocus, Ceratosaurus and 42 other genera.

references.authors: Mannion, P. D.; Upchurch, P.; Schwarz, D.; Wings, O.
references.title: Taxonomic affinities of the putative titanosaurs from the Late Jurassic Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania: phylogenetic and biogeographic implications for eusauropod dinosaur evolution
references.journal: Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society
references.notes: Gives the span: "the Late Jurassic (Oxfordian-Tithonian) Morrison Formation of the western USA".

references.authors: Kirkland, J. I.; Suarez, M.; Suarez, C.; Hunt-Foster, R.
references.title: The Lower Cretaceous in east-central Utah — the Cedar Mountain Formation and its bounding strata
references.notes: Dates the top with a U-Pb age of "148.96 +2.54 to -2.21 Ma" from an ash about 9 m below the Naturita Formation and an age of 150.00 ± 0.52 Ma near the top of the Brushy Basin Member.

references.authors: Chure, D. J.
references.title: A new species of Allosaurus from the Morrison Formation of Dinosaur National Monument (UT-CO) and a revision of the theropod family Allosauridae
references.notes: Works at "Kimmeridgian, Jurassic" throughout for the Salt Wash Member, the horizon of the material it describes.

references.authors: Darton, N. H.
references.title: Geology of the Bighorn Mountains
references.journal: United States Geological Survey Professional Paper
references.notes: Places the formation in the Bighorn uplift on the Cretaceous side of a then-open question: "From stratigraphic evidence in other regions, the Morrison formation is provisionally classed in the early Cretaceous." Of its saurian remains, "Opinions are divided as to whether these are of late Jurassic or early Cretaceous age."

references.authors: Cifelli, R. L.; Davis, B. M.; Sames, B.
references.title: Earliest Cretaceous mammals from the western United States
references.notes: Gives the formation as "mainly Kimmeridgian–Tithonian", possibly reaching into the late Oxfordian and early Berriasian, after Kowallis and colleagues (1998) and Miall and colleagues (2008).

references.authors: Kowallis, B. J.; Christiansen, E. H.; Deino, A. L.; Peterson, F.; Turner, C. E.; Kunk, M. J.; Obradovich, J. D.
references.title: The age of the Morrison Formation

references.authors: Miall, A. D.; Catuneanu, O.; Vakarelov, B. K.; Post, R.
references.title: The Western Interior Basin
references.book: The Sedimentary Basins of the United States and Canada (Miall, A. D., ed.), Sedimentary Basins of the World 5

references.authors: Marsh, O. C.
references.title: Notice of new dinosaurian reptiles from the Jurassic formation
references.notes: Names the deposits for their sauropods: "The deposits which contained them may be called the Atlantosaurus beds, from their most characteristic fossils".

references.title: A new sauropod dinosaur from the Ojo Alamo Formation of New Mexico
references.notes: Uses the two names as one unit: "the Morrison formation (Atlantosaurus beds) of the west".

Brushy Basin.description: The Brushy Basin Member is a member of the Morrison Formation in the United States, dated to the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic. It consists mainly of mudstone. Dinosaurs known from it include Allosaurus, Camarasaurus, Ceratosaurus, Diplodocus and 13 other genera.

references.authors: Carrano, M. T.; Benson, R. B. J.; Sampson, S. D.
references.title: The phylogeny of Tetanurae (Dinosauria: Theropoda)
references.notes: Allosaurus occurs in the "Salt Wash and Brushy Basin Members, Morrison Formation; Kimmeridgian–Tithonian, Late Jurassic", a span given for the two members together. Ceratosaurus comes from the "lower Brushy Basin Member, Morrison Formation; Kimmeridgian–Tithonian, Late Jurassic", and Marshosaurus from the "Brushy Basin Member, Morrison Formation; Kimmeridgian, Late Jurassic".

references.authors: Chure, D. J.
references.title: A new species of Allosaurus from the Morrison Formation of Dinosaur National Monument (UT-CO) and a revision of the theropod family Allosauridae
references.notes: Uses "Brushy Basin Member, Morrison Formation" with "AGE: Kimmeridgian, Late Jurassic" for the material it describes.

references.authors: Kowallis, B. J.; Christiansen, E. H.; Deino, A. L.; Peterson, F.; Turner, C. E.; Kunk, M. J.; Obradovich, J. D.
references.title: The age of the Morrison Formation
references.notes: Dates the member by 40Ar/39Ar on sanidine from ash beds. The ages "range systematically between 148.1 ± 0.5 (1 std. error of mean) at the top of the member to 150.3 ± 0.3 Ma near the bottom", Kimmeridgian at the base and Tithonian at the top on the ICS chart v2024/12 (Tithonian base 149.2 Ma). The paper reads the member as Kimmeridgian–Tithonian on the timescales of its day, and calls one Montezuma Creek age, 147.82 ± 0.63 Ma, about 1 Ma too young. Source of the lithology.

references.authors: Kirkland, J. I.; Suarez, M.; Suarez, C.; Hunt-Foster, R.
references.title: The Lower Cretaceous in east-central Utah — the Cedar Mountain Formation and its bounding strata
references.notes: Relays "150.00 ± 0.52 Ma from near the top of the Brushy Basin Member, near little Cedar Mesa, Emery County, Utah, based on a recalibrated 40Ar/39Ar age (Trujillo and Kowallis, 2015)", Kimmeridgian on the ICS chart v2024/12, and concludes that "the top of the Morrison Formation dates to the lower third of the Tithonian Stage". Places the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary "just above the highest smectitic mudstone beds of the Brushy Basin Member".

references.title: Recalibrated legacy 40Ar/39Ar ages for the Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation, Western Interior, U.S.A.

Salt Wash.lithology: gray or brown sandstone, with less red and green mudstone
Salt Wash.description: The Salt Wash Member is a member of the Morrison Formation in Utah and Wyoming, United States, dated to the Oxfordian to Kimmeridgian stages of the Late Jurassic. It consists mainly of gray or brown sandstone, with less red and green mudstone. Dinosaurs known from it include Allosaurus and Camptosaurus.

references.authors: Carpenter, K.; Wilson, Y.
references.title: A new species of Camptosaurus (Ornithopoda: Dinosauria) from the Morrison Formation (Upper Jurassic) of Dinosaur National Monument, Utah, and a biomechanical analysis of its forelimb
references.notes: Dates Reed's Quarry 13 at Como Bluff, in the member, "latest Oxfordian-earliest Kimmeridgian" from "regional correlations from dated horizons", the quarry lying "about 35 m below the 156.3 + 2 Ma age for strata at the level of Reed's Quarry 9".

references.title: Cranial anatomy of Allosaurus jimmadseni, a new species from the lower part of the Morrison Formation (Upper Jurassic) of Western North America
references.notes: Gives a holotype horizon in "the Salt Wash Member of the Upper Jurassic (Kimmeridgian) Morrison Formation", with referred specimens "in the stratigraphically equivalent lower part of the Morrison Formation in Wyoming".

references.authors: Chure, D. J.
references.title: A new species of Allosaurus from the Morrison Formation of Dinosaur National Monument (UT-CO) and a revision of the theropod family Allosauridae
references.notes: Independently gives "the Salt Wash Member of the Morrison Formation (Kimmeridgian, Jurassic)" at Dinosaur National Monument, the quarry being "Kimmeridgian in age (Kowallis et al. 1998)".

references.authors: Carrano, M. T.; Benson, R. B. J.; Sampson, S. D.
references.title: The phylogeny of Tetanurae (Dinosauria: Theropoda)
references.notes: Pairs it with its neighbor above across the formation's span, "Salt Wash and Brushy Basin Members, Morrison Formation; Kimmeridgian-Tithonian".

references.authors: Kowallis, B. J.; Christiansen, E. H.; Deino, A. L.; Peterson, F.; Turner, C. E.; Kunk, M. J.; Obradovich, J. D.
references.title: The age of the Morrison Formation
references.notes: Cited by Chure (2000) for the Kimmeridgian age of the Dinosaur National Monument quarry. Source of the lithology.

Hongqin.description: The Hongqin Formation is a formation in Anhui, China, dated to the Middle Jurassic. Dinosaurs known from it include Anhuilong and Huangshanlong.

references.title: A new sauropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic of Huangshan, Anhui Province
references.notes: Middle Jurassic of Shexian, Huangshan, Anhui, and the source of the first Jurassic dinosaur described from the province.

references.authors: Ren, X. X.; Huang, J. D.; You, H. L.
references.title: The second mamenchisaurid dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic of Eastern China
references.notes: Purple sandstones interbedded with purple shales in the Tunxi Basin of Anhui, assigned to the Middle Jurassic on invertebrates.

references.authors: Li, N.; Zhang, X.; Ren, X.; Li, D.; You, H.
references.title: A new eusauropod (Dinosauria, Sauropodomorpha) from the Middle Jurassic of Gansu, China

references.notes: Lists the formation among the Middle Jurassic units of China that yield mamenchisaurids.

Snow Hill Island.description: The Snow Hill Island Formation is a formation in Antarctica, dated to the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous. It includes the Cape Lamb Member and the Gamma Member. Dinosaurs known from it include Antarctopelta, Imperobator, Morrosaurus and Trinisaura.

references.title: Unenlagiid affinities for Imperobator antarcticus (Paraves: Theropoda): paleobiogeographical implications
references.notes: Gives "Snow Hill Island Formation (Cape Lamb Member, Lower Maastrichtian ...)".

references.authors: Pittman, M.; O'Connor, J.; Tse, E.; Makovicky, P.; Field, D. J.; Ma, W.; Turner, A. H.; Norell, M. A.; Pei, R.; Xu, X.
references.title: The fossil record of Mesozoic and Paleocene pennaraptorans

references.series: Bulletin of the American Museum of Natural History

references.notes: Tabulates the formation as Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian.

references.authors: Soto-Acuña, S.; Vargas, A. O.; Kaluza, J.
references.title: A new look at the first dinosaur discovered in Antarctica: reappraisal of Antarctopelta oliveroi (Ankylosauria: Parankylosauria)

references.authors: Coria, R. A.; Salgado, L.; Gasparini, Z.; Moly, J. J.

Gamma.lithology: fine- to medium-grained silty sandstone and carbonaceous mudstone, with conglomerate lenses
Gamma.description: The Gamma Member is a member of the Snow Hill Island Formation in Antarctica, dated to the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous. It consists mainly of fine- to medium-grained silty sandstone and carbonaceous mudstone, with conglomerate lenses. It is also known as the Herbert Sound. Dinosaurs known from it include Antarctopelta and Trinisaura.

references.authors: Ely, R. C.; Case, J. A.
references.title: Phylogeny of a new gigantic paravian (Theropoda; Coelurosauria; Maniraptora) from the Upper Cretaceous of James Ross Island, Antarctica

references.authors: Soto-Acuña, S.; Vargas, A. O.; Kaluza, J.
references.title: A new look at the first dinosaur discovered in Antarctica: reappraisal of Antarctopelta oliveroi (Ankylosauria: Parankylosauria)
references.notes: Uses the Snow Hill Island reading, referring osteoderms to "the Campanian-Maastrichtian Gamma Member of the Snow Hill Island". Source of the lithology.
